input: Electric vehicle fast-charging networks in the United States
title: Electric vehicle fast-charging networks in the United States
report:
# Electric Vehicle Fast-Charging Networks in the United States

**Direct answer:** The U.S. public DC fast-charging (DCFC) network has roughly 75,000-78,000 ports depending on the database used, and it is still growing at over 1,000 ports per month - but the *rate* of new construction has fallen year-over-year for two consecutive quarters [2][8][9][12]. Tesla remains the dominant single network at roughly half of all ports, yet its share of *new* builds has fallen from above 40% in 2025 to 26-27% in the first two quarters of 2026 as automaker-backed and retailer-backed entrants scale up [2][10][15]. The strategic battleground has shifted from raw port count to reliability, connector standardization on NACS, ultra-fast hardware, and - most acutely - profitability [2][12][21].

---

## MARKET AT A GLANCE

**Definition.** DC fast charging (also called Level 3) delivers direct current at 50-350+ kW, sitting above Level 1 (120V AC) and Level 2 (240V AC) in the broader charging-station ecosystem, which spans residential, workplace/retail, public fast charging, and fleet depot applications [5]. A "port" powers only one vehicle at a time even if it carries multiple connectors [8].

**Installed base.** Two credible trackers give different totals, and the gap matters:

- **Paren** counted **77,776 ports across 14,514 stations** at the end of Q2 2026, with **4,382 new ports and 806 new stations** added in the quarter [2].
- The **Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC)** counted **74,265 ports across an estimated 15,632 locations** as of July 1, 2026 (up 27% year-over-year), and **75,293 ports** as of July 28, 2026 [8][9].

The two databases have diverged before: one tracker noted a roughly 2,000-stall difference between Paren's end-2025 figure and AFDC's [6]. AFDC also counts temporarily unavailable ports (864, or 1.2%, on July 1, 2026) and warns its station count may be inflated because adjacent chargers are sometimes logged separately [8]. Treat the totals as a range, not a settled number.

**Growth rate.** AFDC-based reporting puts average expansion at over 1,000 new ports per month, and the July 28, 2026 total of 75,293 represents a **50% jump from the 50,000 ports counted in mid-December 2024** [9]. Site size is rising: average ports per AFDC location reached 4.75 on July 1, 2026, up from 4.4 a year earlier [8].

**But the build rate is decelerating.** Paren's Q2 2026 additions (4,382 ports) were **10% below Q2 2025's 4,865**, and first-half 2026 additions of 7,903 ports were **7.4% below the 8,532 added in H1 2025** [12]. Paren itself calls a two-quarter year-over-year decline "not definitive proof of a slowdown," but pairs it with "recent CPO layoffs and pullbacks" [12].

**Market value forecasts diverge sharply** and should be treated as vendor estimates, not facts. IMARC values the U.S. EV *charging station* market (all levels) at **$3.20 billion in 2025**, reaching **$34.20 billion by 2034** at a **28.60% CAGR** [5]. Precedence Research puts 2025 at **$22.52 billion**, reaching **$190.45 billion by 2035** at a **23.8% CAGR** [16]. The roughly seven-fold gap in the 2025 base year implies fundamentally different scope definitions; the material provided here does not include the methodologies behind either. IMARC's segmentation is more useful than its headline: commercial applications hold **63.4%** of 2025 share, Level 2 retains the largest charging-level share at **49.5%**, and Level 3 DC fast is the fastest-growing level at roughly **35.2% CAGR** (2026-2034), with the West region leading at **36.7%** [5].

**Technology mix.** Ultra-fast is becoming default: approximately **62% of new non-Tesla ports** in Q2 2026 supported 250 kW or higher (up from 39% a year earlier), and including Tesla, roughly **72%** of all new ports offered at least 250 kW [2]. NACS reached **22.9% of new non-Tesla ports** in Q2 2026, more than double its ~10% share a year earlier - but CCS still accounts for **70.8% of new non-Tesla builds** and nearly three-quarters of the installed non-Tesla base, versus just 8% for NACS, so "full parity between the two standards remains years off" [2].

---

## KEY PLAYERS

Port counts below come from two databases with different totals; both are given where available.

**Tesla Supercharger** - The largest network: **38,733 ports (49.8% of all-time ports)** per Paren at end-Q2 2026, or **37,159 ports (50% share)** per AFDC on July 1, 2026 [2][8]. All stalls use NACS; more than two-thirds of North American stalls are open to non-Tesla EVs, some via built-in NACS-to-CCS1 "Magic Dock" adapters [8]. Tesla builds far larger sites - **12.1 ports per station** in Q2 2026 versus 4.4 for non-Tesla operators [2]. Peak speed is quoted as 250 kW (V3) to up to 350 kW (V4) [13]; one comparison site instead claims V4 goes to 500 kW [4]. Independent testing cited by one source measured 230 kW achieved on V3 and 235 kW on V4, with 10-80% times of 19 and 18 minutes [22]. Pricing is per kWh (per minute in a few states), demand-priced by time of day, typically **~$0.30-0.45/kWh, up to ~$0.60 at peak/congested sites** [13][18][26]; another tracker cites **$0.42 - $0.49/kWh** non-member with no membership required [17], while a third quotes **~$0.25 - $0.50/kWh** [4]. Tesla does not sell an all-you-can-charge subscription in North America, though an optional membership lowering per-kWh price exists in some regions, especially for non-Tesla EVs [26].

**Electrify America** (Shell-owned, Volkswagen Group-backed [4]) - The largest non-Tesla network: **5,185 ports (6.7% all-time share)** per Paren, or **5,743 ports (7.7%)** per AFDC [2][8]. Highway-corridor focused with 350 kW hardware capable of fully using 800V platforms [4]. Supports CCS and NACS [18]. Pricing is per kWh, roughly **$0.43-0.60**, with **Pass+ (~$7/mo)** cutting the rate about 25% and dropping the session fee [18]; Electrify America's own page confirms Pass+ saves "about 25%" and that pricing varies by charger location and plan, with possible idle fees [24]. A separate tracker cites **$0.48/kWh** non-member with Pass+ at $7.99/mo reducing the rate ~20% [17] - the membership fee and discount figures are not consistent across sources.

**EVgo** (Nasdaq: EVGO) - **3,963 ports (5.1%)** per Paren; AFDC lists **5,208 ports (7%) including Pilot & Flying J** [2][8]. EVgo describes itself as having more than 1,200 fast charging stations across 47 states, deployed with retailers, grocery stores, restaurants, shopping centers, gas stations, rideshare operators, and autonomous vehicle companies [1][7]. Positioning is urban/suburban rather than long-haul [4]. Pricing is per kWh on CCS and NACS, roughly **$0.31-0.4…** per one comparison [18]; another cites **$0.28 - $0.32/kWh** non-member with an **EVgo+ membership at $6.99/mo** [17]; a third cites **~$0.40 - $0.55/kWh** and a "ReVolt" subscription at $7.99/mo [4]. These figures conflict and the material does not reconcile them.

**ChargePoint** - **4,713 ports (6.1%)** per Paren, **4,848 (6.5%)** per AFDC [2][8]. Critically, ChargePoint does not own most of its ports; they belong to thousands of individual owners or companies [6][8]. Its overall connector footprint (over 70,000) is the largest by count but majority Level 2, best suited to workplace, hotel and residential dwell-time charging rather than road-trip fast charging [4]. Pricing is host-set: per kWh where permitted, per minute otherwise, at **$0.49 - $0.69/kWh for DC fast** non-member [17].

**IONNA** - The eight-automaker joint venture (BMW, GM, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, Toyota) [13][3]. **1,201 ports (1.5%)** per Paren, **1,190 (1.6%)** per AFDC, and **1,375 ports across 150 stations** as of mid-August 2026 per its CEO [2][8][3]. Peak speed up to 400 kW, both connectors [13]. Its "Rechargery" sites combine fast chargers with canopies, restrooms, food and lounges; it uses Alpitronic hardware with in-house software and measures reliability by first-attempt success rate [3].

**Retailer and fuel-retail entrants** - **Walmart** added 368 ports in Q2 2026 (8.4% of quarterly additions) off a base of 612, the fastest-growing challenger [2]. **Red E** added 315 ports to reach 1,974 (Paren) or 2,037 (AFDC) [2][8]. **Pilot Flying J** added 146 ports (1,279 total) [2]; the Pilot - GM - EVgo partnership passed **300 fast-charging locations and 1,300 stalls across 40 states**, and EVgo has more than 900 Pilot travel-center locations to draw on across the parent network [1][2].

**Others in the top ranks:** Blink (2,123 ports per Paren; 2,039 per AFDC), EV Connect (1,793), Ford Charge (1,258), Rivian Adventure Network (1,065, crossed 1,000 in June 2026), Mercedes-Benz HPC (872 per Paren; 724 per AFDC), Francis Energy (884), EVCS (847) and BP Pulse (796) [2][8].

---

## RECENT MOVES

- **EVgo × Tesla (Aug 5, 2026):** EVgo will add "EVgo Superchargers" - V4 units capable of **up to 500 kW / 1000 V**, adding up to 200 miles in 15 minutes - to its metropolitan network under Tesla's Supercharger for Business program, which lets third parties own Tesla-built and Tesla-operated hardware [7][20]. Sites will carry Magic Dock for native CCS *and* NACS charging without an adapter, longer cables, and will appear in Tesla's in-car navigation and Trip Planner [7]. Deployments start in fall 2026, first sites operational in H2 2026 [7]. EVgo says demand on its network has risen over 700% in three years and cites more than 35 NACS-equipped models expected by end-2026 and over 3 million Teslas already sold in the U.S. [7]. EVgo also expects first units of a next-generation architecture from its El Segundo Innovation Lab by end of year [7].
- **IONNA tops JD Power (Aug 2026):** IONNA scored **807/1,000** in the 2026 JD Power U.S. EV Experience Public Charging Study, ahead of Mercedes-Benz Charging Network (797) and Rivian Adventure Network (755) - the first year all three were eligible, and all three took the top spots [3]. Newer automaker-backed networks scored especially well on ease of charging, charging speed and charger availability, in some cases more than 100 points above segment average [3].
- **Electrify America white-label (Aug 2026):** Electrify America formalized a third-party white-label program, "Powered by Electrify America," with **Wawa branding eight Electrify America sites in Pennsylvania**; it has built host-owned networks since 2020 via Electrify Commercial, with Costco, WS Development, the New York Power Authority and Rocky Mountain Power among earlier customers [14].
- **Retreats:** Engie and Enel X both left the U.S. market in 2024; Shell said in December 2024 it would stop supporting licensed charging software to focus on its own retail locations, and scaled back further in August 2025 [21].
- **Federal funding disruption:** A February 6, 2025 Federal Highway Administration memorandum suspended state EV infrastructure deployment plans and rescinded related guidance, effectively barring "no new obligations" until guidance was updated; a large portion of NEVI funds remained without approved obligations at the time of the freeze [23].

---

## HOW THEY DIFFER

**Three distinct positioning models are now visible.** Paren's guest analyst frames it as a "Charging 2.0" phase: newer players (Ionna, Walmart, Red E, Mercedes-Benz HPC, Pilot Flying J) are "aggressively building national footprints," while Tesla, Electrify America and EVgo increasingly use "retail clustering" - adding stations inside existing urban markets to capture more share of charge [2]. Layered on that is a *destination-quality* model: JD Power found DC fast chargers at hotels scored highest (692), followed by gas stations/convenience stores (689) and restaurants (688), versus 570 at dealerships and 606 at stand-alone lots and garages - which explains why IONNA, Mercedes-Benz and Rivian invest in site design and amenities [3].

**Moats.** Tesla's is vertical integration and scale: it designs, owns and operates its stalls and ships failing hardware for same-day repair, which one comparison calls the biggest single differentiator, with consistently 99%+ reported uptime [22][4]. Its 12.1-ports-per-station average is nearly triple the non-Tesla figure, which reduces queueing risk at any given site [2]. IONNA's moat is capital and demand from eight automakers plus an explicit reliability metric (first-attempt success rate) [3]. ChargePoint's is the opposite of ownership: an asset-light footprint owned by thousands of hosts, which limits its control over quality but also its capital exposure [6][8].

**Switching costs are falling - and Tesla is monetizing that.** The historical lock-in was the connector. That is eroding from both sides: non-Tesla networks are adding NACS alongside CCS rather than replacing it [2], Magic Dock lets CCS vehicles use Tesla hardware natively [8], and EVgo's Supercharger deal means Tesla hardware will sit inside a competitor's network and appear in Tesla's own navigation [7]. The residual switching costs are now soft: app/RFID accounts, subscription break-even points (Electrify America's Pass+ at ~$7-7.99/mo; EVgo+ at $6.99/mo), and OEM-bundled credits - some GM vehicles include free EVgo charging credits, and BMW and Mini owners get discounted IONNA rates [18][17][4]. None of these approaches the hardware lock-in of five years ago.

**Price is not a strong differentiator.** Headline non-member DC fast rates cluster between roughly $0.28 and $0.69/kWh across networks, with typical DC fast cost cited at **$0.35 - $0.60/kWh** - about $26 - $45 for a 75 kWh battery, or roughly 300 miles of range [25][17][18][13]. The sources disagree on individual network ranges, likely reflecting location-, time- and plan-dependent pricing that Electrify America explicitly acknowledges [24]. Differentiation is therefore running through reliability, siting and amenities, not per-kWh price.

---

## RISKS & OPEN QUESTIONS

**Profitability.** Paren's own read is that the industry's "new mantra" is "operations, customer experience, and profitability," cited alongside CPO layoffs and pullbacks [12]. The 2024 exits of Engie and Enel X and Shell's 2024-2025 retrenchment are concrete evidence that operators with charging experience elsewhere could not make U.S. economics work [21].

**Build-rate deceleration.** Two consecutive quarters of year-over-year declines in new ports (−10% in Q2 2026, −7.4% for H1) sit uneasily against still-rising totals [12]. Whether this is a pause or an inflection is genuinely unresolved in the material.

**Policy.** The February 6, 2025 FHWA memorandum suspended state deployment plans with a large share of NEVI funds not yet obligated [23]. NEVI's $5 billion highway-corridor mandate (stations every 50 miles on designated corridors, with 150+ kW capability at federally funded sites) and the IRA Section 30C 30% credit are cited as structural demand drivers [5] - which makes them structural risks if disrupted.

**Reliability gap.** Failed charging visits fell to **12%** in the most recent quarter measured, from 14% a year earlier and the lowest since the study began in 2021 - still roughly one unsuccessful visit in eight, which JD Power's reporting notes is short of gas-station reliability [3]. Overall DC fast satisfaction rose 12 points to 666, with charger availability up 27 points, perceived safety up 18 and charging cost up 18 [3]. Public Level 2 satisfaction moved the other way, down 12 points to 595 on payment and session-start problems [3]. The study drew on 6,594 BEV and PHEV owners surveyed January - June 2026 [3]. Electrify America's reliability is described as improving but still materially below Supercharger, historically with one-quarter to one-third of chargers showing outage or error at a given visit [4] - a strong claim from a single comparison site, and worth discounting accordingly.

**Connector transition timing.** With NACS at only 8% of the installed non-Tesla base and CCS still 70.8% of new non-Tesla builds, mixed-connector infrastructure and adapters will govern access for years [2].

**Data quality.** Paren and AFDC disagree by roughly 2,000-3,500 ports, and AFDC recorded an unexplained ~580-stall month-over-month *drop* in Tesla stalls in June 2026 that the tracker itself could not account for [6][8]. Any single port figure should be read as an estimate.

---

## BOTTOM LINE

The U.S. fast-charging market has crossed from a land-grab into a consolidation-and-execution phase: capacity keeps compounding toward 75,000-78,000 ports, but new-build volume is down year-over-year and the operators winning credit are those scoring on reliability and site quality rather than raw count [2][12][3]. Tesla's structural advantages - half of all ports, sites nearly three times larger than rivals', and the highest reported uptime - remain intact even as its share of new builds has fallen to 26-27% [2][8][22][10]. The most consequential development is that Tesla is now licensing its hardware to competitors like EVgo, which simultaneously entrenches NACS, dissolves the connector-based moat, and turns Tesla into a supplier to the very networks challenging it [7][20]. Investors should weigh the credible demand signals against the plain evidence that this business has not yet proven it can earn a return: two European entrants and one oil major have already retreated [21].

---

*Not covered by the material: the material provided here does not include current financial results or net income for Blink, ChargePoint or EVgo (beyond EVgo's stated network growth), utility interconnection or grid-upgrade cost data, medium/heavy-duty and megawatt-charging deployment figures, funding rounds or M&A valuations, or state-level pricing regulation detail beyond the note that some states require per-minute billing.*

sources.snippet:

That cost will add approximately 300 miles of range to an electric car (on average).
